concept.name: Config vs Secrets Separation

relationships.description: Connects Config vs Secrets Separation to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Strictly decoupling non-sensitive runtime configuration (feature flags, timeouts, hosts) from sensitive credentials (API keys, DB passwords, TLS private keys) with distinct storage, encryption, and rotation lifecycles.
spark.keyTakeaway: Store config declaratively in Git-tracked ConfigMaps, but inject secrets exclusively at runtime via KMS-backed secret managers and short-lived dynamic leases.

concept.whyItMatters: Treating database passwords or signing keys like ordinary environment config leads to `.env` files committed to Git, secrets leaked in CI logs or crash dumps, and 365-day static credentials that are impossible to rotate without coordinated downtime. Separating config from secrets lets teams iterate on timeouts and feature flags via GitOps pull requests while isolating credentials behind IAM, envelope encryption, and audit trails.
whenToUse: Any production application running in Kubernetes, ECS, or serverless environments that connects to databases, payment gateways, or third-party APIs.
GitOps workflows (ArgoCD, Flux) where manifests are stored in Git repositories accessible to all developers.
Multi-tenant or regulated systems (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA) requiring cryptographic audit logs and 24-hour credential rotation.
whenNotToUse: Ephemeral local unit-test mocks using synthetic throwaway values (`test-secret-123`) that have zero access to real infrastructure.
Publicly distributable client-side bundle identifiers (e.g., public OAuth `client_id` or Google Analytics measurement ID) that are not actually secret.
Over-engineering dynamic Vault leases for truly static public endpoints like `PAYMENT_API_BASE_URL` or `LOG_LEVEL`.
keyPoints: Classification boundary: Config varies by environment and is safe to log or commit to Git (`LOG_LEVEL`, `DB_HOST`, `POOL_SIZE`); Secrets grant identity, decryption, or billing authority (`DB_PASSWORD`, `JWT_PRIVATE_KEY`, `STRIPE_SK`).
Never store plaintext or base64-encoded Kubernetes `Secret` manifests in Git—base64 is encoding, not encryption; use External Secrets Operator (ESO) or SOPS + KMS/age.
Prefer dynamic short-lived credentials (HashiCorp Vault DB secrets engine, AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts / IRSA, SPIFFE X.509 SVIDs) over static API keys.
Mount secrets via memory-backed `tmpfs` files (`/var/run/secrets/...`) rather than OS environment variables when possible, preventing leaks via `/proc/<pid>/environ` or child-process dumps.
Enable etcd encryption at rest with a cloud KMS provider so Kubernetes `Secret` objects are never written in plaintext to disk snapshots.

examples.title: Dynamic PostgreSQL Credentials via HashiCorp Vault
examples.scenario: A 40-microservice platform shared a single static `postgres_prod` password across `.env` files and Kubernetes Secrets, making rotation risky and violating SOC 2.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Vault's Database Secrets Engine with Kubernetes Auth generates unique per-pod Postgres roles (`v-k8s-orders-a8f2`) with a 1-hour TTL and 24-hour max TTL. Leaked credentials auto-expire within 60 minutes and audit logs trace every query to a specific pod identity.

examples.title: GitOps Sync with External Secrets Operator (ESO)
examples.scenario: An engineering team uses ArgoCD to deploy services and needs non-sensitive feature flags in Git without exposing Stripe and SendGrid API keys.
examples.outcome: Non-sensitive settings live in plaintext `ConfigMap` YAML in Git, while an `ExternalSecret` CRD references AWS Secrets Manager keys. ESO syncs encrypted secrets directly into the cluster using IRSA, keeping Git 100% secret-free.

tradeOffs.factor: Static Encrypted Git vs. Runtime Secret Manager
tradeOffs.pro: SOPS-encrypted files in Git keep config and secrets versioned atomically in the same pull request.
tradeOffs.con: Runtime stores (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) support instant revocation, dynamic leases, and access auditing without Git commits.

tradeOffs.factor: Env Vars vs. tmpfs File Mounts
tradeOffs.pro: Environment variables are universally supported by 12-Factor frameworks with zero file-watching code.
tradeOffs.con: File mounts on `tmpfs` support hot rotation without pod restarts and cannot be accidentally dumped by debug endpoints printing `os.environ`.

tradeOffs.pro: 1-hour dynamic DB credentials drastically shrink the blast radius of any credential leak.
tradeOffs.con: Applications must handle lease renewal or connection-pool refresh before TTL expiration to avoid sudden auth failures.

failureModes.name: Crash-Dump & Debug Env Leakage
failureModes.description: Frameworks or error trackers (Sentry, crash reporters, `/actuator/env`) serialize `process.env` or `System.getenv()`, exposing API keys in log aggregators.
failureModes.mitigation: Mount secrets as `tmpfs` files, scrub sensitive keys in logger/APM redaction filters, and disable `/actuator/env` in production.

failureModes.name: Rotation Auth Storm
failureModes.description: Rotating a shared database password or API key in Secrets Manager without dual-key grace periods immediately breaks all running pods until restarted.
failureModes.mitigation: Use dual-active key rotation (primary + secondary key), dynamic per-pod credentials, or hot-reloadable file watchers.

failureModes.name: Secret Store Cold-Start Outage
failureModes.description: If Vault or Secrets Manager is unreachable during an autoscaling spike, new pods fail to start because they cannot fetch boot-time credentials.
failureModes.mitigation: Run HA multi-AZ secret stores, use local Vault Agent caching, and decouple non-critical secrets from liveness/startup probes.

failureModes.name: Base64 GitOps Illusion
failureModes.description: Engineers commit standard Kubernetes `kind: Secret` YAML to Git assuming base64 `data:` fields are safe, permanently exposing credentials in Git history.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce pre-commit and CI secret scanners (Gitleaks, TruffleHog) and block raw `kind: Secret` manifests in GitOps admission controllers.

commonMistakes: Passing secrets as Docker `ARG` or `ENV` instructions inside a `Dockerfile`, baking credentials permanently into immutable OCI image layers.
Putting non-sensitive URLs or feature flags inside Secrets Manager, hitting API rate limits and paying per-secret fees unnecessarily.
Leaving Kubernetes `etcd` unencrypted at rest, allowing anyone with snapshot access to read all cluster Secrets in plaintext.
Forgetting to purge Git history (`git filter-repo`) and rotate the exposed credential immediately after an accidental commit—deleting the line in a new commit leaves it in history.
Using a single wildcard IAM role for all microservices instead of least-privilege per-service secret paths.

sections.content:
## The idea

The Twelve-Factor App popularized storing configuration in the environment, but modern production security requires splitting that environment into two distinct planes: **Configuration** (non-sensitive behavior tuning like timeouts, pool sizes, and feature flags) and **Secrets** (cryptographic material, passwords, and API tokens that grant access or authority). Configuration belongs in version-controlled declarative files for reproducibility and diffability; secrets belong in dedicated KMS-backed vaults with strict IAM scoping, memory-only injection, audit logging, and automated rotation.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider deploying an `invoice-worker` microservice to Amazon EKS that reads from PostgreSQL and calls Stripe:

1. **Config Plane (Git)**: `configmap.yaml` holds `DB_HOST=orders-rw.internal`, `HIKARI_MAX_POOL=12`, `STRIPE_TIMEOUT_MS=2000`, and `ENABLE_PDF_V2=true`. Any engineer can review and merge changes via GitHub PR.
2. **Identity Plane (Zero Static Keys)**: Instead of storing AWS access keys, the pod's Kubernetes `ServiceAccount` uses IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) to exchange a short-lived OIDC JWT for temporary AWS STS credentials.
3. **Secrets Plane (Runtime Injection)**: External Secrets Operator (or Secrets Store CSI Driver) authenticates with AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault, pulls the Stripe key and requests a dynamic 1-hour Postgres role, and mounts them onto a memory-backed `tmpfs` volume at `/var/run/secrets/app/` (`0400` permissions).
4. **Application Read**: On startup (and on `SIGHUP`/file-watch), the app reads `/var/run/secrets/app/stripe_key` without ever placing the string into `os.environ`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Static vs. dynamic secrets and workload identity
sections.content:
## Static vs. dynamic secrets and workload identity

The gold standard for secrets management is **eliminating static long-lived secrets wherever possible**:
- **Workload Identity Federation (IRSA, GCP Workload Identity, SPIFFE/SPIRE)**: Services authenticate to cloud APIs and each other using short-lived cryptographic tokens (OIDC JWTs or X.509 SVIDs rotated every 15–60 minutes) bound to the pod's namespace and service account.
- **Dynamic Database Secrets**: Instead of a shared static password, Vault creates a unique database user per pod (`CREATE ROLE ... VALID UNTIL ...`) and revokes it automatically when the lease expires.
- **Envelope Encryption**: When secrets must be stored (e.g., third-party webhook HMAC keys), a Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts the secret, and a cloud KMS Key Encryption Key (KEK) wraps the DEK—allowing key rotation and instant revocation via KMS policy.

## Secret delivery mechanism comparison

| Mechanism | Storage & Encryption | Rotation Support | Leak Risk | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Plaintext `.env` / K8s Secret in Git** | Base64 in Git & etcd | Manual redeploy | Critical (Git history, `/proc/environ`) | Never use in production |
| **SOPS + KMS / age in Git** | AES-GCM encrypted values in Git | Requires PR + KMS re-encrypt | Low in Git; medium if injected as env vars | Small teams wanting pure GitOps without Vault |
| **External Secrets Operator (ESO)** | AWS/GCP Secret Manager -> K8s Secret | Automated polling (e.g., 1h) | Medium unless etcd KMS encryption is enabled | Standard Kubernetes teams on AWS/GCP/Azure |
| **Vault Agent / CSI `tmpfs` + Dynamic Leases** | Vault encrypted storage + RAM-only mount | Seamless dynamic per-pod TTLs (1h) | Lowest (never in etcd, disk, or env vars) | Regulated, high-security, multi-cloud platforms |

## Failure modes

- **Stale credential after rotation**: Applications that read a secret file once at `main()` startup fail with `401 Unauthorized` or `28P01` when a secret rotates in-place. Implement file-watch reload or dual-key grace periods.
- **CI/CD pipeline exfiltration**: Printing `env` in GitHub Actions or passing secrets on CLI flags (`curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`) exposes credentials in build logs and `ps aux` output.
- **Over-broad IAM policies**: Granting a pod `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `*` instead of `arn:...:secret:prod/orders/*` lets a single compromised dependency read every service's keys.
- **Docker layer caching leaks**: Copying `.env` or passing `--build-arg NPM_TOKEN` during `docker build` leaves secrets recoverable via `docker history` even if deleted in a later `RUN` step.

## Audit, scanning, and drift prevention

Enforcement must be automated across both the build pipeline and runtime:
- **Pre-commit & CI Scanning**: Run `gitleaks` or `trufflehog` on every PR and push to block high-entropy strings, AWS key prefixes (`AKIA...`), and private key headers (`-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----`).
- **Admission Control**: Use Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper to reject Kubernetes pods that define literal `env[].value` matching secret patterns or mount host paths.
- **CloudTrail / Vault Audit Logs**: Alert when a secret is accessed by an unexpected IAM role, from outside the production VPC, or when a revoked lease is attempted.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify every runtime parameter: move non-sensitive hosts, timeouts, and flags to `ConfigMap`/Git; move all credentials to a secret manager.
- [ ] Enable `etcd` envelope encryption at rest with cloud KMS on all Kubernetes clusters.
- [ ] Replace static cloud IAM keys with OIDC Workload Identity (IRSA / GKE WI / SPIFFE).
- [ ] Mount secrets via `tmpfs` (`Secrets Store CSI` or Vault Agent) instead of environment variables where supported.
- [ ] Enable `gitleaks` in pre-commit hooks and CI, plus automated secret-scanning alerts on GitHub/GitLab.
- [ ] Test secret rotation end-to-end in staging with zero pod restarts or dropped connections.

interviewProblems.title: Config vs Secrets Separation
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Config vs Secrets Separation. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Strictly decoupling non-sensitive runtime configuration (feature flags, timeouts, hosts) from sensitive credentials (API keys, DB passwords, TLS private keys) with distinct storage, encryption, and rotation lifecycles.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: CSI / ESO Agent applies the primary invariant and coordinates with App Pod.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, App Pod experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Mount secrets as `tmpfs` files, scrub sensitive keys in logger/APM redaction filters, and disable `/actuator/env` in production.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Store config declaratively in Git-tracked ConfigMaps, but inject secrets exclusively at runtime via KMS-backed secret managers and short-lived dynamic leases.
Avoid trap: Passing secrets as Docker `ARG` or `ENV` instructions inside a `Dockerfile`, baking credentials permanently into immutable OCI image layers.
Avoid trap: Putting non-sensitive URLs or feature flags inside Secrets Manager, hitting API rate limits and paying per-secret fees unnecessarily.
When to reach for it: Any production application running in Kubernetes, ECS, or serverless environments that connects to databases, payment gateways, or third-party APIs.
When to reach for it: GitOps workflows (ArgoCD, Flux) where manifests are stored in Git repositories accessible to all developers.

putItTogether.title: Putting Config Secrets Separation Together
putItTogether.summary: Store config declaratively in Git-tracked ConfigMaps, but inject secrets exclusively at runtime via KMS-backed secret managers and short-lived dynamic leases.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Config Secrets Separation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Migrating to Vault's Database Secrets Engine with Kubernetes Auth generates unique per-pod Postgres roles (`v-k8s-orders-a8f2`) with a 1-hour TTL and 24-hour max TTL. Leaked credentials auto-expire within 60 minutes and audit logs trace every query to a specific pod identity.
